rows.stem: Three friends A, B and C got their photograph clicked. Find the probability that B is standing at the central position, given that A is standing at the left corner.
rows.solution: Three friends standing in a row can be arranged in \(3! = 6\) ways, so the sample space is \(S = \{ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA\}\), each arrangement read as (left, centre, right) and each equally likely. Let \(E_1\) be the event that B stands at the central position and \(E_2\) the event that A stands at the left corner. The arrangements with A at the left are \(ABC\) and \(ACB\), so \(P(E_2) = \dfrac{2}{6}\). Of these, only \(ABC\) also has B in the centre, so \(P(E_1 \cap E_2) = \dfrac{1}{6}\). By the definition of conditional probability, \(P(E_1 \mid E_2) = \dfrac{P(E_1 \cap E_2)}{P(E_2)} = \dfrac{1/6}{2/6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Hence the required probability is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) -- which makes sense, since fixing A at the left leaves B equally likely to take either of the two remaining places.

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: If the area of the region bounded by the line \(y = mx\) and the curve \(x^2 = y\) is \(\dfrac{32}{3}\) sq. units, then find the positive value of m, using integration.
rows.solution: The area is not given as a number to compute but as a condition on \(m\), so set up the integral in terms of \(m\) and then solve. The curve \(x^2 = y\) is the upward parabola \(y = x^2\) and \(y = mx\) is a line through the origin. They meet where \(mx = x^2\), that is \(x(x - m) = 0\), so the \(x\)-coordinates of intersection are \(0\) and \(m\). For \(m > 0\) the line lies above the parabola on \([0, m]\), so the enclosed area is \(\int_{0}^{m} \left(mx - x^2\right) dx = \left[\dfrac{mx^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{m} = \dfrac{m^3}{2} - \dfrac{m^3}{3} = \dfrac{m^3}{6}\). Equating this to the given area, \(\dfrac{m^3}{6} = \dfrac{32}{3}\), so \(m^3 = \dfrac{32 \times 6}{3} = 64\) and therefore \(m = 4\). Hence the positive value of \(m\) is \(4\).

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) and the projection of vector \(\vec{c} + \lambda \vec{b}\) on vector \(\vec{a}\) is \(2\sqrt{6}\), then find the value of \(\lambda\).
rows.solution: The projection of a vector \(\vec{u}\) on \(\vec{a}\) is \(\dfrac{\vec{u} \cdot \vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}\), so the given condition reads \(\dfrac{(\vec{c} + \lambda\vec{b}) \cdot \vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|} = 2\sqrt{6}\). First, \(|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{6}\). Expanding the dot product by linearity, \((\vec{c} + \lambda\vec{b}) \cdot \vec{a} = \vec{c} \cdot \vec{a} + \lambda(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a})\), where \(\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a} = (1)(2) + (3)(-1) + (-1)(1) = 2 - 3 - 1 = -2\) and \(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} = (1)(2) + (1)(-1) + (-2)(1) = 2 - 1 - 2 = -1\). Substituting, \(\dfrac{-2 + \lambda(-1)}{\sqrt{6}} = 2\sqrt{6}\), so \(-2 - \lambda = 2\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{6} = 12\). Hence \(-\lambda = 14\), giving \(\lambda = -14\).

The factor \(\dfrac{1}{1 + e^x}\) is neither even nor odd, but the limits are symmetric, so use \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-a}^{a} f(-x)\,dx\) and add. Let \(I = \int_{-3}^{3} \dfrac{x^4}{1 + e^x}\,dx\) ... (1). Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\), and noting \((-x)^4 = x^4\), gives \(I = \int_{-3}^{3} \dfrac{x^4}{1 + e^{-x}}\,dx\). Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(e^x\), \(I = \int_{-3}^{3} \dfrac{e^x x^4}{1 + e^x}\,dx\) ... (2). Adding (1) and (2), the awkward denominator cancels: \(2I = \int_{-3}^{3} \dfrac{x^4\left(1 + e^x\right)}{1 + e^x}\,dx = \int_{-3}^{3} x^4\,dx\). Now \(2I = \left[\dfrac{x^5}{5}\right]_{-3}^{3} = \dfrac{243}{5} - \left(-\dfrac{243}{5}\right) = \dfrac{486}{5}\), so \(I = \dfrac{243}{5}\). Hence the value of the integral is \(\dfrac{243}{5}\).
